claims.text: The initial FeCoNi alloy is single-phase FCC.
Single-phase FCC FeCoNi has high saturation magnetization.
The coercive field of the initial single-phase FCC FeCoNi is at or below 100 Oe.
Controlled annealing can induce nanometer-scale ordered second-phase precipitation within an FCC FeCoNi matrix.
Annealing temperature can control the formation and length scale of phase decomposition.
Annealing duration can be optimized to control nanoscale precipitation in FeCoNi.
An inert or controlled atmosphere will prevent oxidation during annealing.
The post-annealing cooling rate can preserve the desired precipitate distribution.
The annealed material will contain uniformly dispersed nanoscale ordered precipitates, potentially B2-like, embedded in an FCC matrix.
Precipitate-matrix interfaces act as magnetic domain-wall pinning sites.
Pinning domain walls at precipitate-matrix interfaces increases coercivity.
Nanoscale precipitation can increase coercivity while only minimally reducing saturation magnetization.
The annealed FeCoNi will have a coercive field substantially above 100 Oe relative to untreated FeCoNi.
The annealed FeCoNi will retain high saturation magnetization.
Excessive precipitate growth or coarsening may reduce saturation magnetization.
Excessive annealing may cause unwanted phase transformations.
The magnetic response depends on the alloy's precise stoichiometry and microstructural evolution.
TEM and XRD can be used to assess precipitate formation and retention of the FCC matrix, while magnetometry can measure coercivity and saturation magnetization.

contradictions.description: The intervention is thermal annealing, but the experiment instructs characterization of the 'irradiated microstructure'; no irradiation step is specified, making the experimental description internally inconsistent.
